query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of Nb into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will improve its long‐term creep and corrosion resistance under service conditions without compromising its established strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with a fine lamellar microstructure consisting of fcc and B2 phases
generation.intervention: Alloy modification via microalloying by adding approximately 2–5 atomic percent Nb during melting and casting
generation.conditions: Evaluation under cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (creep at room temperature), and controlled corrosive environments (e.g., saline exposure); standard tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures for mechanical property verification
generation.structural_mediator: Nb is expected to segregate at the lamellar phase boundaries and/or form very fine secondary precipitates, thus reinforcing the interfacial regions between the fcc and B2 phases
generation.mechanism: By locally strengthening the phase interfaces, Nb addition should retard diffusion and boundary sliding that facilitate creep under constant stress and prevent degradation of the passive film, thereby enhancing resistance against both long-term mechanical deformation and corrosive attack
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-doped alloy is predicted to show a reduced creep strain rate and lower corrosion rates while maintaining a similarly high fracture strength and ductility compared to the baseline alloy
generation.baseline: The conventional AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA exhibits a fine lamellar structure with superior room-temperature and high-temperature tensile properties but limited documented performance under prolonged mechanical loading and corrosive conditions
generation.boundary: Improvement is expected within the specified Nb concentration range and under moderate environmental aggressiveness; excessive Nb or different service conditions could lead to unwanted phase formation or compromised ductility
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Nb content and the quantitative extent of improvements in creep and corrosion behavior remain uncertain, necessitating experimental verification under realistic operational conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of alloys: one set of standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and another set with 3 atomic percent Nb added. Subject both sets to accelerated room-temperature creep tests under constant load and cyclic exposure to a saline solution. Characterize the mechanical properties via tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures, and use high-resolution microscopy to assess microstructural changes, especially at phase boundaries.
measurements: Creep strain rate and total creep strain over a set time period
Corrosion rate (e.g., via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy or weight loss measurement)
Tensile strength and ductility (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Microstructural analysis (phase distribution and Nb segregation using SEM/TEM or atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped alloy shows no statistically significant improvement in creep resistance or corrosion rate compared to the baseline, or if its strength–ductility balance deteriorates (e.g., marked reduction in ductility or increased brittleness), then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
